lead: Searching answers one question: where is this value in the list, and is it there at all? Sorting puts a list in order so later work gets easier. You meet both constantly — a roll number in a class list, a name in your phone contacts. This chapter writes two searches in Python, compares their costs, and shows how Python sorts a list and how a simple exchange sort works by hand. Linear search checks items one by one; binary search throws away half the list at every step and needs the list sorted first.
prereq: You need: 3.3 Lists for indexing, len and slicing, and Unit 2 for while and for loops.

sections.h3: Linear search: compare items one at a time

blocks.text: Linear search starts at index 0 and compares each item with the target, returning the index of the first match. If nothing matches, it returns -1 as a "not found" signal. Real positions run from 0 to n-1, so -1 never collides with a position that was actually found. Careful: Python allows negative indexing, so a[-1] is the last item — always test the returned value against -1 before using it as an index. A few syllabi call this sequential search.

items: If i has reached len(a), stop and return -1.
Compare a[i] with the target; if they are equal, return i.
Add 1 to i and repeat from step 2.

blocks.text: Cost: one comparison in the best case (target at index 0), n in the worst case, where n = len(a), when the target is last or absent, and about n/2 on average. Time is O(n): double the list and the work roughly doubles. Linear search needs no sorted data, so it works on any list.
These versions return a pair (index, comparisons); index is the position of the first match, or -1 when the target is absent. The counter is added only to show the cost.
The run returns index 999 after 1000 comparisons, and -1 after 1000 comparisons for a value that is not there.

sections.h3: Binary search: halve a sorted list

blocks.text: Binary search works only on a sorted list. It looks at the middle item and discards the half that cannot hold the target, so one comparison removes half the remaining items and the work grows with log₂ n instead of n.

blocks.where: low and high are the first and last indices of the part still in play; // is floor division, so mid is a whole-number index.

items: While low ≤ high, compute mid = (low + high) // 2.
If a[mid] equals the target, return mid.
If a[mid] < target, the target can only lie to the right: set low = mid + 1.
When low > high the part is empty: return -1.

blocks.text: Each comparison halves the count: n → n/2 → n/4 → ... → 1. That is log₂ n halvings, so about log₂ n comparisons in the worst case. For n = 1000, log₂ 1000 ≈ 9.97, about 10 comparisons against 1000 for linear search. The price is that the list must already be sorted.
Same 1000 items, same targets: 10 and 9 comparisons instead of 1000.

sections.h3: Sorting: list.sort(), sorted(), bubble sort and selection sort

blocks.text: Python sorts two ways. L.sort() rearranges the list in place and returns None. sorted(L) builds a new sorted list and leaves L untouched. Both accept reverse=True and key=, a function whose return value is used for comparison.

blocks.code:
marks = [("Asha", 78), ("Ravi", 92), ("Meera", 65)]
marks.sort(key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True)
print(marks)
print(sorted([3, 1, 2]))
nums = [3, 1, 2]
out = nums.sort()
print(nums, out)

blocks.text: Read the last line twice: nums.sort() returned None, so nums = nums.sort() would wipe out the list. Python's sort is Timsort, a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort: it finds short sorted runs, extends them by insertion sort, then merges them. Worst case n log₂ n comparisons, best case n on already-sorted data.
Bubble sort swaps neighbours that are out of order and repeats until a full pass makes no swap. On [5, 1, 4, 2]:

Selection sort finds the smallest item, swaps it to the front, and repeats on the rest: [5, 1, 4, 2] → [1, 5, 4, 2] → [1, 2, 4, 5]. Both are O(n²), taught to show the idea; Python's built-in sort beats them on real data.

sections.h3: Best, average and worst case at a glance

blocks.text: n is the number of items; log₂ n is the base-2 logarithm.
Bubble sort reaches n in the best case only when the pass stops as soon as no swap happens.

figure.caption: 21 is smaller than 27, so the left half is dropped; 33 is larger, so the right half is dropped; the next middle is 27 itself, found in three comparisons.

examples.question: L = [3, 9, 14, 21, 27, 33, 40]. Search for 27 with linear search and with binary search. Give the index and the number of comparisons for each. Then state how many comparisons each search needs for 1,000 items in the worst case.
steps: Linear search: compare a[0] = 3 (no), a[1] = 9 (no), a[2] = 14 (no), a[3] = 21 (no), a[4] = 27 (yes). 5 comparisons, index 4.
Binary search: low = 0, high = 6, mid = (0 + 6) // 2 = 3. a[3] = 21 < 27, so low = 4. 1 comparison.
low = 4, high = 6, mid = 5. a[5] = 33 > 27, so high = 4. 2 comparisons.
low = 4, high = 4, mid = 4. a[4] = 27, match. 3 comparisons, index 4.
1,000 items: linear search needs up to 1,000 comparisons; binary search needs about ⌈log₂ 1000⌉ = 10, since 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≥ 1000.
examples.answer: Linear search finds 27 at index 4 in 5 comparisons; binary search finds it at index 4 in 3 comparisons. For 1,000 items the worst case is 1,000 comparisons against about 10.
examples.check:
import math
L = [3, 9, 14, 21, 27, 33, 40]
target = 27

def linear(a, t):
    c = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        c += 1
        if a[i] == t:
            return i, c
    return -1, c

def binary(a, t):
    low, high, c = 0, len(a) - 1, 0
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        c += 1
        if a[mid] == t:
            return mid, c
        if a[mid] < t:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1, c

i1, c1 = linear(L, target)
i2, c2 = binary(L, target)
print(c1)
print(i1)
print(c2)
print(i2)
print(math.ceil(math.log2(1000)))

traps: Binary search on an unsorted list returns a wrong answer with no error message. Sort first, or use linear search.
Writing low = mid instead of low = mid + 1 can loop forever: when low meets high, mid equals low and the range never shrinks.
L.sort() returns None. The line L = L.sort() leaves L as None and the next statement crashes.
Sorting just to run one binary search costs n log₂ n, more than one linear search at n. Sorting pays off only when you search the same list many times.
Always check the returned index against -1 before indexing: a[-1] is a legal Python item, not an error.

quiz.q: State in one sentence what linear search does and what it returns when the target is absent.
quiz.a: It compares the target with each item from index 0 onwards and returns the index of the first match, or -1 if no item matches.

quiz.q: Why must the list be sorted before a binary search?
quiz.a: The decision to drop the left or the right half depends on order: a[mid] < target must guarantee the target lies to the right. In an unsorted list that guarantee is false, so whole halves may be discarded wrongly.

quiz.q: L = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]. Trace binary search for 12: give low, high, mid, the comparison, and the final index with the comparison count.
quiz.a: low = 0, high = 6, mid = 3, a[3] = 8 < 12, so low = 4 (1 comparison). low = 4, high = 6, mid = 5, a[5] = 12, match (2 comparisons). Index 5 after 2 comparisons.

quiz.q: What does this print? nums = [4, 1, 3]; out = nums.sort(); print(out, nums)
quiz.a: None [1, 3, 4]. sort() sorts in place and returns None, so out is None while nums is sorted.

quiz.q: A program must search a list of 10,000 items 5,000 times. Compare 5,000 linear searches with sorting once and then binary searching 5,000 times.
quiz.a: Linear: 5,000 × 10,000 = 5 × 10⁷ comparisons. Sorted route: sorting about n log₂ n ≈ 10,000 × 13.3 ≈ 1.3 × 10⁵, plus 5,000 × 14 = 7 × 10⁴, total about 2 × 10⁵. Sorting once is roughly 250 times cheaper here.

quiz.q: Why is bubble sort's best case n but its worst case n²?
quiz.a: On already sorted data one pass makes no swaps and stops, so n - 1 comparisons. In reverse order every pass swaps many pairs and n - 1 passes are needed, giving about n²/2 comparisons, which is O(n²).

quiz.q: Why does a failed search return -1 rather than 0?
quiz.a: 0 is a real position (the first item), so it cannot signal failure. -1 lies outside the range 0 to n-1, so it cannot be mistaken for a found position. The caller must still check for -1 before using the result as an index, because Python reads a[-1] as the last item.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production sorts are tuned hybrids: Python ships Timsort, C++ libraries use introsort, Java uses dual-pivot quicksort for primitives. Binary search hides inside database indexes, where B-trees generalise it to many-way splits, and inside git bisect. Python's bisect module gives binary search directly. Comparison sorting cannot beat n log₂ n comparisons in the worst case.
